title: Pediatric Headaches: Migraine, Tension-Type and Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension
subject: ss-paediatric-neurology
module: Congenital Malformations, Hydrocephalus and Raised ICP

steps.say: Childhood migraines differ distinctly from adult presentations with shorter durations and frontotemporal distribution.
steps.tx: Apply ICHD-3 criteria to recognise **Pediatric migraine duration and localization** in school-age children and adolescents. Pediatric migraines are notably briefer in duration than adult attacks, lasting between 2-72 hours (compared to >= 4 hours in adults). Furthermore, headache pain is commonly bilateral (frontotemporal or bifrontal) rather than strictly hemicranial, presenting with a throbbing, pulsatile quality aggravated by routine physical activity, and accompanied by photophobia, phonophobia, nausea, or episodic vomiting (Triptan licensing in pediatric acute migraine).

left.title: Pediatric Migraine (ICHD-3)
points: Duration: 2-72 hours (shorter than adults)
Location: frequently bilateral (bifrontal or bitemporal)
Gastrointestinal: intense nausea, abdominal discomfort
Relief: sleep is highly restorative and often terminates attack

right.title: Adult Migraine
points: Duration: 4 to 72 hours
Location: strictly unilateral hemicranial pain (> 60%)
Aura: visual scintillating scotoma more prevalent
Chronification: strongly associated with medication overuse

steps.tx: School age **pediatric migraine** is shorter than adult migraine, lasting 2 to 72 hours rather than 4 hours or longer. Pain is commonly bilateral, frontotemporal or bifrontal, not strictly one sided. It throbs, worsens with ordinary activity, and comes with photophobia, phonophobia, nausea or spells of vomiting. ICHD 3 criteria are used to recognise that pattern. The dark room and the bilateral overlay match this childhood distribution rather than a strictly hemicranial adult attack.
steps.say: Childhood migraine often lasts 2 to 72 hours, shorter than the adult attack that runs 4 hours or more. Pain is commonly bilateral across forehead and temples, throbbing, worse with activity, and joined by light and sound sensitivity, nausea or vomiting. That bilateral pattern, not a one sided adult headache, is what the criteria look for.

vis.alt: A school age child lies in a darkened room with eyes closed, holding the forehead, while a head overlay marks bilateral frontal and temporal pain and a shaded window indicates photophobia.
vis.caption: A child rests in the dark with a hand on the forehead, bilateral frontal and temporal pain marked on a head overlay, and the window shaded for light sensitivity. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.say: Specific triptan nasal sprays and tablets hold paediatric regulatory approvals based on child age.
steps.tx: Review age-stratified **Triptan licensing in pediatric acute migraine** when formulating rapid abortive treatment. Oral rizatriptan (5-10 mg; specifically 5 mg for weight 20-40 kg and 10 mg for weight > 40 kg) is approved for children >= 6 years of age taken immediately at headache onset. For adolescents >= 12 years, intranasal triptans provide rapid transmucosal absorption bypassing gastric stasis: nasal sumatriptan (5-20 mg nasal spray) and nasal zolmitriptan (2.5-5 mg nasal spray) are approved abortive options (CHAMP trial in migraine prophylaxis).

rows: 5-10 mg (5 mg for 20-40 kg, 10 mg for > 40 kg) at onset
5-20 mg single nasal spray into one nostril
2.5-5 mg single nasal spray into one nostril

steps.say: The randomized CHAMP trial demonstrated that common preventive medications offered no benefit over placebo in youth.
steps.tx: Incorporate findings from the **CHAMP trial in migraine prophylaxis** when discussing preventative therapy with families. The landmark NIH-funded multicenter CHAMP randomized trial evaluated amitriptyline, topiramate, and placebo in children aged 8-17 years with frequent migraines. The trial showed no statistically significant difference in headache frequency reduction between either active drug and placebo (all groups showed > 50% relative reduction), while active drugs caused significantly higher adverse events. Consequently, first-line prevention emphasizes cognitive behavioral therapy, regular sleep hygiene, hydration, and meal schedules (Cyclic vomiting and abdominal migraine).

left.title: CHAMP Trial Findings
points: No difference in 50% reduction between amitriptyline (52%), topiramate (55%), and placebo (61%)
Topiramate caused significant cognitive slowing and paresthesias
Amitriptyline caused fatigue, dry mouth, and weight gain
Strong placebo response (~60%) in pediatric trials

right.title: First-Line Lifestyle & Behavioral Focus
points: Strict sleep hygiene (consistent bedtime and wake time)
Hydration (1.5-2 L water daily) and regular unskipped meals
Cessation of daily caffeine and energy drinks
Cognitive behavioral therapy and biofeedback relaxation

steps.say: Childhood periodic syndromes include cyclic vomiting and abdominal migraine that respond to cyproheptadine.
steps.tx: Diagnose episodic **Cyclic vomiting and abdominal migraine** as classic childhood periodic precursors to migraine. Abdominal migraine manifests as recurrent, paroxysmal midline abdominal pain lasting 2-72 hours, accompanied by pallor, flushing, anorexia, and headache. Cyclic vomiting syndrome features stereotypical bouts of relentless, intractable vomiting (>= 4 emetic episodes per hour) lasting hours to days separated by symptom-free intervals. Prophylaxis with the antihistaminic/antiserotonergic agent cyproheptadine (0.25-0.5 mg/kg/day) or pizotifen demonstrates high efficacy in younger children (Idiopathic intracranial hypertension Friedman criteria).

rows: Midline periumbilical pain, pallor, anorexia, headache
Predictable bouts of intractable vomiting (>=4/hr), dehydration
Cyproheptadine, coenzyme Q10, L-carnitine, amitriptyline (>10 yr)
Sudden recurrent brief vertigo attacks, nystagmus, ataxia

steps.say: Definite pseudotumour cerebri requires papilloedema normal imaging and elevated lumbar puncture opening pressure.
steps.tx: Apply the **Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) Friedman criteria** to establish diagnosis of pediatric pseudotumor cerebri syndrome. Definite IIH mandates the presence of bilateral papilledema, a completely normal neurological examination (with the sole exception of a unilateral or bilateral abducens nerve 6th palsy), normal brain MRI and MR venography excluding mass lesions and sinus thrombosis, normal CSF composition, and an elevated lumbar puncture opening pressure >= 28 cmH2O measured in a calm, non-crying, recumbent child (or >= 25 cmH2O if non-sedated/non-obese) (Acetazolamide dosing in pediatric IIH).

vis.alt: Fundus image of papilloedema showing a swollen optic disc with blurred margins and engorged veins in a child
vis.caption: Fundus image of papilloedema with blurred disc margins and venous engorgement in a child. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.say: High dose acetazolamide serves as the medical mainstay to suppress cerebrospinal fluid production.
steps.tx: Prescribe targeted **Acetazolamide dosing in pediatric IIH** as the first-line pharmacotherapeutic cornerstone. Acetazolamide acts by reversibly inhibiting carbonic anhydrase within the choroid plexus epithelium, curtailing active CSF production by up to 50%. In pediatric patients, it is initiated at 20-25 mg/kg/day divided into three doses and aggressively up-titrated as tolerated across a 20-100 mg/kg/day range up to a maximum daily dose of 2-4 g/day. Patients must be monitored for metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia, paresthesias, gastrointestinal distress, and nephrolithiasis (Secondary causes of raised ICP without mass).

rows: Baseline serum electrolytes, urea, creatinine, and venous bicarbonate
Serial visual field perimetry; track fundoscopic papilledema grade
Supplemental sodium bicarbonate or potassium citrate if serum HCO3 < 18

steps.say: Reviewing medication exposures uncovers secondary triggers of intracranial hypertension including tetracyclines.
steps.tx: Screen for **Secondary causes of raised ICP without mass** before concluding primary idiopathic disease. Secondary pseudotumor cerebri syndrome in children is frequently triggered by specific pharmacologic exposures, including tetracycline-class antibiotics (minocycline, doxycycline used for adolescent acne), excessive or withdrawal of systemic corticosteroids, hypervitaminosis A and retinoids (isotretinoin), recombinant human growth hormone therapy, and lithium. In addition, magnetic resonance venography must meticulously rule out cerebral venous sinus thrombosis and internal jugular vein compression (Optic nerve sheath fenestration vs shunting).

left.title: Medication & Metabolic Triggers
points: Tetracyclines (doxycycline, minocycline for acne)
Hypervitaminosis A and synthetic retinoids (isotretinoin)
Corticosteroid withdrawal or prolonged high-dose therapy
Recombinant human growth hormone therapy

right.title: Vascular & Systemic Triggers
points: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (transverse/sagittal)
Severe iron deficiency anemia (impairs CSF resorption)
Systemic lupus erythematosus and antiphospholipid syndrome
Addison disease and hypoparathyroidism

steps.say: When vision is failing despite medical therapy urgent optic nerve sheath fenestration or shunting is necessary.
steps.tx: Weigh **Optic nerve sheath fenestration vs shunting** when children experience progressive visual field constriction or failing visual acuity despite maximum medical therapy. Optic nerve sheath fenestration (ONSF) involves creating small dural incisions behind the globe to decompress the retrobulbar subarachnoid space; it is ideal for rapidly deteriorating vision with minimal headache. In contrast, ventriculoperitoneal (VP) or lumboperitoneal (LP) shunting rapidly lowers global intracranial pressure, relieving both severe intractable headache and papilledema, though carries lifelong risks of shunt obstruction and infection.

rows: Progressive visual field loss; stable headache
Direct optic nerve decompression; avoids permanent foreign shunt hardware
Effective global ICP reduction; stereotactic navigation into small ventricles
Alternative when ventricular cannulation is hard
Avoids cranial entry; higher risk of low-pressure headache and revision
